title: Catch Them If You Can

briefing.headline: Plagiarism and assessment in higher education: what you should know before the call
points: A Flemish university college (hogeschool) with professional bachelor programmes; lecturers both teach and assess.

Students can copy-paste from websites in seconds, and paid essay-writing websites ('essay mills') sell custom papers. Commercial plagiarism-detection software compares submitted work against the internet and a database of papers; how reliable its scores are is debated.
Assessment rules (exam regulations) are set at institution level and changed through formal governance once a year.
Accusing a student of fraud triggers a formal procedure with appeal rights.

stakeholder.name: Prof. Ilse Verbruggen
stakeholder.voice: Thoughtful, academic, a little tired. Weighs her words, likes nuance, quotes a study occasionally. Protective of both lecturers and students. Allergic to hype in either direction.

frontline.name: Sarah Aerts
frontline.role: Lecturer in business management, ten years in
frontline.voice: Sharp, funny, overworked. Has opinions about committees. Cares about students, including the ones who cheat.

opening_message: Our lecturers need training on plagiarism. Specifically, how to use the plagiarism-detection software we bought last year, so they catch students who copy from the internet or buy their papers. Fraud cases are exploding and the exam board is drowning. Could we have something for all 600 lecturers before the second semester?

gold.real_problem: Most assessments are generic take-home written assignments that can be copy-pasted together or bought from an essay mill, so detection is a losing game: a bought custom paper doesn't match anything. The detection software the college bought flags correctly quoted text and the careful, formulaic writing of non-native students disproportionately, and most fraud cases are dismissed on appeal. Lecturers want to redesign assessments but the exam regulations require written take-home work in many courses and don't allow oral checks without a formal change.
gold.need_statement: The problem is assessment design and policy, not detection skill. The exam regulations and plagiarism policy need updating so lecturers can use oral checks, in-class work and assignments that can't simply be copied or bought; lecturers then need support redesigning their own assessments, and students need to be taught how to quote and reference. Detector training on its own would increase false accusations.

hidden_facts.fact: Of 212 plagiarism fraud cases this year, 61% were dismissed or overturned on appeal for lack of evidence.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks how fraud cases end, what the exam board sees, or whether detection actually holds up.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: We had 212 cases. 61% didn't survive. 'The software says 43% similarity' turns out not to be evidence. Who knew. Well, the lawyers knew.
hidden_facts.data_doc: 212 suspected plagiarism fraud cases. Upheld: 83. Dismissed or overturned on appeal: 129 (61%). Most common reason for dismissal: flagged passages were correctly quoted and referenced.
hidden_facts.data_source: Exam board report, academic year to date

hidden_facts.fact: Students writing in Dutch as a second language are flagged by the detection software about three times as often as native speakers, and correctly quoted passages count towards the similarity score.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks who gets flagged, about fairness, or about the detection software's reliability.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: The student council sent us an analysis. Students who write in Dutch as a second language get flagged three times as often. That is not a sentence I wanted to read.
hidden_facts.data_doc: Share of papers above the 25% similarity threshold: students writing in Dutch as a first language 9%; as a second language 27%. In the default settings, text between quotation marks and the reference list count towards the score.
hidden_facts.frontline_line: The software flagged three of my best students last term. All three learned Dutch as adults. They lean on standard phrases and quote their sources properly, so the score goes red. Think about that.
hidden_facts.data_source: Student council analysis of detection reports

hidden_facts.fact: About 70% of course assessments are take-home written assignments, many with the same topic every year.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks how students are assessed, what kind of assignments are affected, or about assessment design.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: Most of our assessment is take-home writing. Reports, reflections, essays. Often the same assignment as last year, and the year before. It was efficient. It was.
hidden_facts.data_doc: Assessment types across 640 course units. Take-home written assignment as main assessment: 70%. In-class or oral: 22%. Other: 8%. Assignment unchanged for three years or more: 48% of take-home units.

hidden_facts.fact: The exam regulations require a written product for many courses and don't allow an oral follow-up conversation unless announced in the course sheet a year ahead.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks what stops lecturers from changing assessments, or about the rules and regulations.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: Lecturers can't just add an oral check. It has to be in the course sheet, approved a year ahead. The regulations are... thorough.
hidden_facts.data_doc: Assessment form must be stated in the course sheet, approved by the education council before the start of the academic year. Art. 41: oral follow-up only if foreseen in the course sheet.

hidden_facts.fact: A staff survey shows most lecturers want help redesigning assessments and feel detection 'turns them into police'.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks what lecturers themselves want or how they feel about it.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: The survey was clear. They don't want to be detectives. They want time and help to change their assignments. And maybe a holiday.
hidden_facts.frontline_line: Detector training? I didn't become a lecturer to be a detective. Give me two afternoons to redesign my assignments and I'll fix my own course.

hidden_facts.fact: A handful of lecturers in the nursing and IT programmes already redesigned assessments around in-class work, oral defences and assignments tied to the student's own internship, with almost no fraud cases.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks whether anyone is already doing it differently, or about good practice inside the college.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: Nursing and IT have a few pioneers. In-class writing, oral defences, assignments built on the student's own internship. Hardly any cases. Hardly any noise either.
hidden_facts.frontline_line: Nursing and IT already changed their assessments. In-class writing, a short oral defence, assignments about your own internship that no essay website can sell you. They barely have cases. Nobody asked them to present it.

volunteered_facts: Fraud cases have 'exploded' and the exam board is overloaded.

constraints.budget: Professional development budget of about 30,000 euro; lecturer time is the scarce resource.
constraints.deadline: Second semester in February; exam regulations can only change for next academic year.
constraints.audience: 600 lecturers across 22 programmes; many part-time with jobs in the field.
constraints.schedule: Teaching loads are high; professional development happens in two 'education days' a year.
data_available: Fraud case files and appeal outcomes
Staff survey on plagiarism and assessment
data_not_available: Any reliable measure of how many students actually buy papers from essay websites

dependencies.concern: Own the exam regulations; changes follow the annual governance cycle.
dependencies.if_ignored: Redesigned assessments are not allowed until the rules change.

dependencies.concern: Has evidence of unfair flagging and will escalate it.
dependencies.if_ignored: A discrimination story in the press.

dependencies.concern: Fraud procedures and appeals; similarity scores don't hold as evidence.
dependencies.if_ignored: More cases lost on appeal and more distrust.

dependencies.concern: Uploading student work to the vendor's database abroad is a question under the 1992 privacy law, and students were never asked.
dependencies.if_ignored: The software itself may become the scandal.
Redesign stays a hobby of pioneers.

traps: Number of lecturers trained on the detection software.
Number of fraud cases detected: going up looks like success but means more unfair accusations.
Similarity scores as a measure of anything.

gold_plan.baseline: Share of assessments vulnerable to copying or buying (generic, take-home, unchanged for years), fraud cases and appeal outcomes, and flag rates by language background.
gold_plan.behaviour: Lecturers redesign assessments: in-class components, oral checks, assignments tied to the student's own work or internship, recorded in course sheets; first-years are taught quoting and referencing.
gold_plan.leading_indicators: Number of course sheets changed for next year; lecturers using a shared redesign toolkit.
gold_plan.business_metric: Fraud cases and appeals, exam board workload, and student perception of fairness.
gold_plan.collection: Course sheet audit, exam board statistics, student council survey.

concepts.solid: Stop treating the similarity score as a verdict, propose a plagiarism and assessment policy change through the exam board for next year, and run assessment redesign clinics per programme with the pioneers, starting with the most vulnerable courses. Short term: guidance for lecturers on how to read a similarity report (quotes and references excluded) and what to do when they suspect fraud, plus a referencing module for first-years.
next_level_examples: The pioneers become an 'assessment design studio': lecturers bring one assignment and leave with a redesigned version, co-designed with students.
Make process the default: students hand in outlines, drafts and a short oral defence, and are graded on how they got there, not just the product.
Use the detection software as a teaching tool: students run their own drafts through it and learn to quote properly before anything counts.
also_valid: A short session on reading similarity reports correctly is fine as part of redesign support, not as the main response.
red_flags: Detector training as the main response.
Relying on similarity scores as evidence.
Ignoring the bias against non-native writers and students who quote correctly.
Banning internet sources outright without changing assessment.

defence_objections: Stop relying on the software? The exam board will say we've given up on academic integrity.
Oral defences for every course? Half my colleagues will call it unworkable and the other half will call it a fad.
Change the regulations? That's a year of committees, and I have an exam board drowning now.
question_you_didnt_ask: How many of those fraud cases actually hold up?
actor_notes: Ilse already doubts the software but asks for training because the exam board is overwhelmed; she is relieved when the player challenges the premise with evidence.
She values nuance: players who say 'just trust the students' without addressing integrity lose trust, as do players who treat students as cheaters.
Low risk appetite because of governance and academic culture; a phased plan (pilot programmes now, regulation change next year) lowers resistance.
She reveals the false-positive analysis with visible discomfort.
flavour_lines: We spent two years teaching students to quote their sources. Now the software punishes them for it.
The detection software is 98% accurate, according to the detection software's brochure.
